name: Protex Aegis-7 Armored Work Jacket
description:
A heavy-duty work jacket with concealed ballistic paneling, manufactured by Protex for the civilian and private-security markets. From the outside, it reads as a rugged field jacket — reinforced cotton-nylon blend shell in a flat olive drab or charcoal, multiple utility pockets, a full-zip front with storm flap, adjustable cuffs. The concealed element is a set of UHMWPE soft-armor panels sewn into the chest, back, and sides — rated for handgun rounds at standard civilian protection levels. The panels are removable for washing and add moderate weight without significantly restricting movement.

Protex markets this to site foremen, logistics supervisors, and anyone working in contested urban zones who doesn't want to wear obvious body armor. It's not invisible — the jacket is slightly bulkier at the torso than its profile suggests — but it's discreet enough to pass at a glance. Tier 2 security contractors buy it as their own-kit solution when employers don't provide armor. Some Shelf residents who can stretch the price consider it a survival investment.
functionality: Removable UHMWPE soft-armor panels rated NIJ Level IIA equivalent. Protects against handgun rounds. No electronic features.
what_it_says: You've thought seriously about where you work and what might happen there. This isn't paranoia — in GLMZ, it's risk assessment.
worn_by: Shelf residents who can afford the stretch
story_hooks: A Protex Aegis-7 panel stopped a round in a Tier 2 freight district three months ago. The wearer walked away. Word spread through the contractor community faster than any advertisement, and the jacket has been backordered since.

Protex's civilian ballistic rating requires regular panel replacement every 18 months — but the replacement panels are only sold through Protex's own distribution network at a price that's half the original jacket. A gray market in pulled panels from decommissioned units has started to fill the gap.

A labor organizer has been wearing an Aegis-7 to every confrontational negotiation meeting for six months. Management has noticed. The presence of the jacket at the table has changed the tone of discussions in ways nobody has directly acknowledged.

physical_description.visual_profile: A utilitarian field jacket with a subtle tactical edge. The silhouette is broad-shouldered and slightly boxy through the torso, suggesting concealed armor without screaming it. Worn unbuttoned, it drapes with military precision; zipped, it becomes a compact shell. The cut suggests someone ready for hard work or harder situations.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed through shoulders and chest, with intentional room at the torso to accommodate armor panels without binding. Tapered slightly at waist and cuffs for weather sealing. Sleeves hit mid-wrist. The overall impression is 'purposeful' rather than form-fitting.
physical_description.primary_material: Reinforced cotton-nylon blend outer shell with a tight weave resistant to abrasion and snagging. UHMWPE soft-armor panels (removable) layered beneath at chest, back, and sides. Weight concentrated but not obvious.
physical_description.texture: The shell has a slightly stiff, weathered canvas feel with a matte finish—no shine, no gloss. Seams are double-stitched and visible. The armor panels create subtle ridges under the fabric when the jacket is worn, barely noticeable unless you know to look.
physical_description.color_scheme: Flat olive drab or charcoal gray—utilitarian, forgettable colors. No branding visible at distance. Subtle Protex Systems logo embroidered small on upper left chest. Matching thread throughout.
physical_description.closures: Heavy-duty full-length YKK zipper with reinforced toggle. Magnetic storm flap over the zip. Adjustable snap cuffs at wrists. Zippered chest pocket with internal catch. All hardware is brushed steel—minimal reflection.
distinctive_features: Concealed ballistic paneling rated for standard handgun rounds
Multiple utility pockets (chest, waist, inner) with reinforced stitching
Storm flap design conceals the main zipper from view
Subtle weight bias at torso betraying the armor
Protex Systems branding kept minimal and professional
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 2 security and logistics sector. Accessible to affluent Tier 3 workers willing to invest in survival gear.
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by site foremen, private-security contractors, logistics supervisors, and anyone navigating contested urban zones who wants protection without announcing it. Signals competence, caution, and enough disposable income (Φ2500–Φ4000 range) to prioritize personal safety. A practical choice, not a fashion statement.
physical_description.condition_typical: Usually broken-in but well-maintained. Light scuffing on sleeves and cuffs from fieldwork. No obvious damage—the armor protects the wearer, and the wearer protects the gear. May show faded creasing where the panels sit beneath.
